extracted.intended_audience: school and postsecondary institution administrators, Title IX coordinators, investigators, decisionmakers, and institutional legal counsel responsible for implementing Title IX grievance procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory criteria and procedural requirements governing how recipients must conduct Title IX grievance procedures, including privacy protections, evidentiary rules, notice obligations, and training/appeal mechanisms. Focused on implementing and complying with §§106.2, 106.6, 106.45, 106.46, and 106.8.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable steps to protect privacy (§106.45(b)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must take reasonable steps to protect the privacy of parties and witnesses during the grievance procedures while not taking steps that restrict the parties' ability to obtain and present evidence, consult with family members, confidential resources, or advisors, or otherwise prepare for or participate in the grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balancing privacy and due process: reasonable steps may include withholding identities of parties/witnesses while proceedings are pending; overly restrictive measures that impede evidence-gathering or preparation jeopardize fairness. Restrictions on discussing allegations (e.g., social media or media disclosures) may be permissible if consistent with the First Amendment and do not block ability to obtain/present evidence or consult advisors. Department replaced prior phrasing (e.g., 'prepare for a hearing'/'defend their interests') with 'otherwise prepare for or participate in the grievance procedures' for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment constraint on privacy protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must ensure that measures taken to protect privacy are consistent with the First Amendment; nothing in the Title IX regulations requires a recipient to restrict rights protected from government action by the First Amendment (see §106.6(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should be mindful that privacy-protective restrictions cannot impinge on constitutionally protected speech; limitations (including possible limits on media/social media disclosures) must be tailored to be consistent with First Amendment rights. The regulation does not create a blanket gag order; categorical prohibitions on criticizing a recipient are not a reasonable step to protect privacy, but prohibiting identification of parties/witnesses while procedures are ongoing may be reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice obligations regarding grievance procedures and privacy (e.g., §§106.44(f)(1)(iii), 106.45(c)(1)(i),(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients (through the Title IX Coordinator and notice of allegations) must inform complainants and respondents of the grievance procedures, including what types of evidence and questions are impermissible and must provide notice of allegations that includes the identities of parties involved in the incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulations require recipients to include information about privacy protections and impermissible evidence in the notice of allegations and initial notifications; Title IX Coordinators are obligated to notify parties of grievance procedures upon notification of conduct that may constitute sex discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evaluation of all relevant evidence (§106.45(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures must require a decisionmaker to objectively evaluate all evidence that is 'relevant' (as defined in §106.2), excluding evidence that is impermissible under §106.45(b)(7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department retained the 2020 amendments' language requiring objective evaluation. Parties may raise concerns about relevance as part of their reasonable opportunity to respond (§§106.45(f)(4)(ii), 106.46(e)(6)(ii)). Investigators and decisionmakers receive training on the meaning/application of 'relevant' (§106.8(d)(2)(iv)). The recipient may allow other opportunities for parties to contest relevance determinations; for §106.46 complaints, parties may appeal erroneous relevance determinations that affected the outcome (§106.46(i)(1)(i)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'relevant' (§106.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Relevant' is defined as 'related to the allegations of sex discrimination' and that evidence is relevant when it may aid a decisionmaker in determining whether the alleged sex discrimination occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule cross-references §106.2 for clarity; recipients and trained personnel should apply the ordinary meaning in assessing whether evidence may aid the decisionmaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of impermissible evidence regardless of relevance (§106.45(b)(7))
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain categories of evidence (and questions seeking that evidence) must not be accessed, considered, disclosed, or otherwise used in the grievance procedures even if they are otherwise relevant, subject only to narrow exceptions described in §106.45(b)(7)(i)-(iii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department consolidated and clarified categories of impermissible evidence. Impermissible evidence may be accessed/considered only for the narrow purpose of determining whether an exception under §106.45(b)(7)(i)-(iii) applies. Decisionmakers may consider reasons for partial withholding when assessing credibility. The prohibition is intended to protect particularly sensitive information (e.g., medical records, prior sexual conduct, privileged communications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Privileged evidence and communications with confidential employees (§106.45(b)(7)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must exclude evidence protected under a privilege recognized by Federal or State law and evidence provided to a confidential employee, unless the person to whom the privilege or confidentiality is owed has voluntarily waived the privilege or confidentiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Waivers must be voluntary; the Department removed a prior requirement specifying the manner of waiver tied to jurisdictional standards and instead allows recipients discretion to specify manner (which may include written waiver). If the information is also available from non-confidential sources, it may be accessed from those sources. Recipients are not required by Title IX to advise parties to consult counsel, though parties may choose to do so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Records maintained in connection with treatment (§106.45(b)(7)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Records made or maintained by a physician, psychologist, or other recognized professional or paraprofessional in connection with the provision of treatment to a party or witness must not be accessed, considered, disclosed, or otherwise used in the grievance procedures unless the recipient obtains that party's or witness's voluntary, written consent for use in the grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protection extends to witnesses as well as parties and includes student treatment records such as IEPs and Section 504 plans. The Department declined to create exceptions (e.g., for physical injury relevance). The regulations do not override FERPA/HIPAA; recipients must comply with other applicable laws. The Department recognizes concerns about parties' understanding of waivers but maintains that voluntary consent provides heightened protection for particularly sensitive records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of evidence regarding complainant's sexual interests or prior sexual conduct (§106.45(b)(7)(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence and questions regarding a complainant's sexual interests or prior sexual conduct are presumptively excluded from the Title IX grievance procedures, with two narrow exceptions; prior sexual conduct between the parties does not prove or imply consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declined to adopt an ordinary-relevance or particularized-relevance test for this category given its sensitivity and potential for prejudice and chilling effects; the rule aligns with rape-shield protections. Parties may assert why certain evidence should not be excluded as part of their reasonable opportunity to respond, but determinations are inherently fact-specific. The protection does not extend categorically to respondents; the Department declined to expand exclusions to respondents' history beyond what is necessary for Title IX goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training requirement for investigators, decisionmakers, and implementers (§106.8(d)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators, decisionmakers, and other persons responsible for implementing grievance procedures must receive training on the meaning and application of the term 'relevant' and on the types of evidence that are impermissible regardless of relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required training is intended to promote consistent, fair application (including in elementary and secondary school contexts) and to ensure implementers understand exclusions (privilege, treatment records, sexual history) and how to apply narrow exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural opportunity to contest relevance and appeal adverse relevance determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may raise concerns about relevance determinations as part of their reasonable opportunity to respond to evidence (see §§106.45(f)(4)(ii), 106.46(e)(6)(ii)) and, for §106.46 complaints, may appeal erroneous relevance determinations that affected the outcome (§106.46(i)(1)(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may allow additional opportunities to contest relevance (see §106.45(j)); preserving parties' ability to challenge relevance is part of balancing fairness and privacy protections.
